questions.question: Why must large molecules like proteins and fats be broken down during digestion?
options: Because cells can only use them if they are split into smaller molecules first.
To allow them to be absorbed through the gut wall into the body.
To prevent them from being attacked by helpful bacteria in the stomach.
To make sure they can dissolve in the water inside the mouth.

questions.question: Once nutrients are absorbed into the blood, what is their primary destination and purpose?
options: They are stored permanently in the blood vessels to keep the blood thick.
They are transported around the body to cells that need them.
They are carried directly to the kidneys to be filtered out of the body immediately.
They are taken to the lungs to be mixed with oxygen before entering any cells.

questions.question: Some nutrients can move from the small intestine into the blood by diffusion. Which statement best describes how this happens?
options: Particles move from an area of lower concentration in the intestine to a higher concentration in the blood, requiring energy.
Particles are actively pumped through specialized valves in the intestine wall.
Particles move from an area of higher concentration in the intestine to a lower concentration in the blood.
Particles are carried by water currents through large pores without any concentration difference.

questions.question: Which of the following describes how the lining of the small intestine is adapted to maximize the absorption of nutrients?
options: It is perfectly smooth and thick to prevent nutrients from escaping too quickly.
It has a very large surface area due to finger-like projections called villi.
It is covered in a thick layer of acid-resistant mucus that slows down digestion.
It is extremely short, allowing food to pass through as quickly as possible.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most accurate description of a bacterium?
options: A non-living particle made of proteins and genetic material.
A multicellular organism that lacks a true cellular structure.
A microorganism made of a single living cell.
A specialized human cell designed to fight off infections.

questions.question: Which statement best represents the diversity of bacteria in relation to human health?
options: All bacteria are pathogens that cause harmful infectious diseases.
Some bacteria cause disease, but many are harmless and some are actually helpful.
Bacteria are only helpful to humans and never cause any kind of illness.
Bacteria only become harmful when they are inside the stomach acid.

questions.question: Where in the human body would you find a large population of helpful bacteria that assist with digestion?
options: Inside the salivary glands in the mouth.
Inside the human digestive system.
Inside the windpipe and lungs.
On the dry outer surface of the teeth.

questions.question: How do the helpful bacteria living in our digestive system assist in digesting foods that we cannot digest ourselves?
options: They physically grind the food into smaller pieces using cellular teeth.
They release enzymes that break down these complex food molecules.
They absorb the food whole and carry it directly into our bloodstream.
They produce acid that dissolves the food instantly.

questions.question: In what way do helpful gut bacteria protect us against harmful pathogens that enter our digestive system?
options: They produce antibodies that destroy all foreign cells.
They build physical walls around the pathogens to trap them.
They compete against the pathogens for resources and space.
They signal the brain to raise the body's temperature immediately.

questions.question: Compare mechanical and chemical digestion. Which of the following correctly describes a difference between them?
options: Mechanical digestion only occurs in the stomach, while chemical digestion only occurs in the mouth.
Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces, whereas chemical digestion uses enzymes to break chemical bonds.
Mechanical digestion turns food into completely new substances, while chemical digestion only changes its shape.
Chemical digestion is carried out by muscles, while mechanical digestion is carried out by hormones.

questions.question: What are the three main groups of molecules that make up the food we eat?
options: Minerals, vitamins, and water.
Carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.
Sugars, starches, and fiber.
Enzymes, acids, and saliva.

questions.question: What is the primary role of enzymes during the chemical digestion of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats?
options: They act as fuel to provide energy for the digestive organs.
They act as biological catalysts to speed up the breakdown of these molecules.
They physically squeeze the food to break it into smaller parts.
They lower the temperature of the stomach to prevent burning.

questions.question: According to the digestive processes of the body, what are proteins and fats broken down into, respectively?
options: Sugars and starch.
Fatty acids/glycerol and amino acids.
Amino acids and fatty acids/glycerol.
Carbohydrates and proteins.

questions.question: A student wants to test a food sample to see if it contains starch (a large carbohydrate molecule). Which chemical reagent should they use?
options: Benedict's solution.
Iodine solution.
Biuret reagent.
Ethanol.

questions.question: To test for the presence of simple sugars (small molecules) resulting from the breakdown of starch, which reagent and condition should be used?
options: Iodine solution at room temperature.
Benedict's solution with heating.
Biuret reagent with shaking.
Ethanol mixed with cold water.

questions.question: During a food test experiment, a student adds Biuret reagent to a liquid food sample and observes a color change from blue to lilac/purple. What does this result indicate?
options: The food sample contains a high amount of starch.
The food sample contains protein.
The food sample contains simple sugars.
The food sample contains lipids/fats.

questions.question: Which of the following represents the correct sequence of major organs that food passes through after it is swallowed?
options: Oesophagus -> Stomach -> Small Intestine -> Large Intestine.
Stomach -> Oesophagus -> Large Intestine -> Small Intestine.
Oesophagus -> Small Intestine -> Stomach -> Large Intestine.
Stomach -> Small Intestine -> Oesophagus -> Large Intestine.

questions.question: How is the stomach specifically adapted to carry out its function in the digestive system?
options: It has thin, transparent walls to let light in for chemical reactions.
It has a muscular wall to churn food and produces acid and enzymes to break down food.
It is lined with villi to absorb the majority of digested nutrients into the blood.
It produces bile to neutralize acid before the food enters the mouth.

questions.question: What happens to the parts of the food we eat that cannot be digested by our enzymes or bacteria?
options: They are absorbed into the blood and filtered out by the lungs.
They are converted into liquid urine in the kidneys.
They are passed out of the body as faeces.
They remain in the stomach permanently to help digest future food.

questions.question: A student adds iodine solution to a piece of bread and it turns blue-black. They also heat a sample of milk with Benedict's solution and it remains blue. What can be concluded about the bread and milk?
options: The bread contains starch, and the milk does not contain detectable reducing sugars.
The bread contains protein, and the milk contains starch.
The bread has no starch, and the milk has a high sugar content.
Both the bread and the milk contain large amounts of fat.

questions.question: Why is the chemical breakdown of large food molecules like proteins and fats necessary before they can be used by the body?
options: Large molecules cannot physically pass through the semi-permeable membranes of the digestive tract into the bloodstream.
Large molecules would react chemically with blood plasma and cause clotting.
Large molecules are too heavy for the blood to transport to the body's cells.
Large molecules must be broken down so they can be rebuilt directly into the exact same structures in the stomach.

questions.question: A person absorbs glucose in their small intestine. How does this glucose reach a muscle cell in the leg to provide energy?
options: It travels through specialized lymphatic vessels directly connecting the gut to major muscles.
It is absorbed into the blood and pumped by the heart through blood vessels to the leg cells.
It diffuses slowly through the interstitial fluids of the body from organ to organ.
It is carried by red blood cells which engulf the glucose molecules.

questions.question: During digestion, some nutrients can be absorbed into the blood by simple diffusion. Which condition must be met for this passive process to occur effectively?
options: The nutrient molecules must be small enough and there must be a higher concentration of them in the gut than in the blood.
The nutrient molecules must be large and there must be active transport pumps working in the cell membranes.
The blood must have a higher concentration of the nutrient than the liquid inside the small intestine.
The molecules must be water-insoluble so they can dissolve directly through the muscular wall of the stomach.

questions.question: The lining of the small intestine is folded into thousands of tiny, finger-like projections called villi. How does this structural adaptation directly maximize the rate of nutrient absorption?
options: It increases the surface area over which nutrients can diffuse into the blood.
It muscularly squeezes the food to force nutrients through the intestinal walls.
It lowers the temperature of the intestine so enzymes work more safely.
It increases the volume of the intestinal cavity so more food can be stored.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes a single bacterium living within the human gut?
options: It is a multicellular microorganism that lacks any cellular boundaries.
It is a non-living organic particle that replicates by invading human host cells.
It is a living microorganism made of a single cell that carries out its own life processes.
It is a microscopic eukaryotic cell containing a membrane-bound nucleus and mitochondria.

questions.question: While some bacteria are pathogens that cause illness, how do harmless or helpful bacteria compare to them?
options: Helpful bacteria are always much larger than pathogenic bacteria.
Helpful bacteria do not cause disease and can provide benefits to their host, unlike pathogens.
Harmless bacteria are non-living, whereas pathogens are living organisms.
Harmless bacteria only live on the skin, while pathogens only live in the blood.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the natural habitat and state of helpful bacteria in the human body?
options: They live inside the human digestive system as part of a healthy gut ecosystem.
They are transient invaders that are constantly destroyed by stomach acid and never survive.
They live only inside the liver where they assist in filtering harmful toxins.
They reside inside the red blood cells to assist with oxygen transport.

questions.question: How do helpful gut bacteria assist humans in digesting complex plant materials, such as certain dietary fibers?
options: They physically chew the food using microscopic, tooth-like structures.
They release enzymes that break down chemical bonds in food molecules we cannot digest ourselves.
They absorb the complex molecules whole and convert them into mineral salts.
They produce strong acids that chemically burn the fiber into smaller units.

questions.question: How do helpful bacteria in our digestive system help protect us from harmful pathogens that we might ingest with food?
options: They release antibodies into the bloodstream to neutralize foreign viruses.
They physically block and compete against the pathogens for space and nutrients.
They engulf and digest the pathogens through phagocytosis.
They increase the acidity of the mouth to kill incoming microbes.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs a type of digestion with its description and a primary location where it occurs?
options: Mechanical digestion: breaking chemical bonds using enzymes; occurs mainly in the mouth.
Chemical digestion: physical breaking of food into smaller pieces; occurs mainly in the stomach.
Mechanical digestion: physical breaking of food into smaller pieces; occurs in the mouth and stomach.
Chemical digestion: physical churning of food by muscles; occurs mainly in the small intestine.

questions.question: A student analyzes a meal consisting of grilled chicken, buttered toast, and an egg. What are the three main types of large food molecules that make up this meal?
options: Carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.
Starch, glucose, and amino acids.
Minerals, vitamins, and dietary fiber.
Proteins, enzymes, and nucleic acids.

questions.question: What is the primary role of digestive enzymes during the breakdown of food in the alimentary canal?
options: They act as reactants that are completely consumed to provide energy to the body.
They act as biological catalysts that speed up the chemical digestion of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.
They change the temperature of the stomach to allow chemical reactions to occur.
They mechanically grind large food particles into smaller pieces.

questions.question: According to the digestive processes of the human body, what are the final products of the chemical digestion of proteins, fats, and carbohydrates?
options: Proteins break down into fatty acids, fats into amino acids, and carbohydrates into starch and sugars.
Proteins break down into amino acids, fats into fatty acids and glycerol, and carbohydrates into starch and sugars.
Proteins break down into glycerol, fats into starch, and carbohydrates into amino acids.
Proteins break down into starch and sugars, fats into amino acids, and carbohydrates into fatty acids.

questions.question: A student wants to test a food sample to see if it contains starch. Which chemical reagent should they use, and what is the positive result?
options: Biuret reagent, which turns from blue to purple.
Iodine solution, which turns from orange-brown to blue-black.
Benedict's solution, which turns from blue to brick-red when heated.
Ethanol, which forms a cloudy white emulsion.

questions.question: After incubating starch with amylase (an enzyme) for 30 minutes, a student wants to test if the starch has been broken down into sugars. Which reagent and condition should they use?
options: Iodine solution at room temperature.
Biuret solution at room temperature.
Benedict's solution, heated in a water bath.
Ethanol, shaken and mixed with cold water.

questions.question: A student performs three food tests on a liquid food sample. Iodine test: remains orange-brown. Biuret test: turns purple. Benedict's test (heated): turns brick-red. What does the sample contain?
options: Starch and protein, but no sugar.
Protein and sugar, but no starch.
Starch and sugar, but no protein.
Fat and starch, but no protein.

questions.question: Which of the following represents the correct sequence of major organs that a piece of food passes through after it is swallowed?
options: Oesophagus -> Stomach -> Small Intestine -> Large Intestine
Oesophagus -> Stomach -> Large Intestine -> Small Intestine
Oesophagus -> Liver -> Stomach -> Small Intestine
Stomach -> Oesophagus -> Small Intestine -> Large Intestine

questions.question: How is the stomach specifically adapted to carry out its functions in the digestive system?
options: It has a highly alkaline environment to neutralize any acid produced by gut bacteria.
It has muscular walls to churn food and glands that secrete acid and digestive enzymes.
It is lined with millions of villi to absorb digested nutrients directly into the blood.
It has a very thin, single-cell layer wall to allow rapid diffusion of large fat molecules.

questions.question: What happens to dietary fiber and other materials in our food that cannot be digested by the human body?
options: They are absorbed by the large intestine and converted into energy in the liver.
They are filtered out of the blood by the kidneys and excreted as urine.
They pass through the digestive system and are eliminated from the body as faeces.
They are broken down by stomach acid into carbon dioxide and exhaled.

questions.question: How does the rich network of blood capillaries inside each villus of the small intestine contribute to efficient nutrient absorption?
options: It keeps the temperature of the intestine high enough to melt large fat molecules.
It constantly carries absorbed nutrients away, maintaining a steep concentration gradient for diffusion.
It pumps digestive enzymes directly into the center of the small intestine.
It prevents bacteria from entering the rest of the body by filtering the absorbed food.
